feedback: If the learner closes the gap between objective and slide while looking through the eyepiece: only bring them together while watching from the side, then focus by widening the gap (objective up or stage down).
If the learner tries coarse focus on high power: coarse focus is for low power only; switch to fine focus once magnified.
activities.intendedInsight: Focusing safely means bringing the lens close while watching from the side, then focusing by moving away from the slide — this prevents cracking the slide and damaging the objective.
learnerActions: With the lowest-power objective in place, bring the objective and slide close together (lower the objective or raise the stage, depending on the microscope) while watching from the side (not through the eyepiece).
Then look down the eyepiece and focus by increasing the gap between objective and slide (objective up or stage down, depending on the microscope) using the coarse adjustment on low power.
Switch to the fine adjustment to sharpen the image.
Explain why coarse focus is used only on the lowest power.
activities.title: Safe focusing drill: watch from the side, move the lens away

feedback: For magnification: multiply both lenses; ×10 eyepiece × ×40 objective = 400×, not 40×.
For order: locate and centre on low power before increasing magnification.

For bubble vs cell: an air bubble is often rounder with a thick, dark rim, can shift or merge when the slide is nudged, and tends to lie above the cell layer; confirm against the actual view rather than relying on the outline alone.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the correct order, the safe focusing rule, and the magnification calculation, and can give reasons to distinguish an artefact from a real structure.
learnerActions: Put the steps of using a microscope in the correct order.
Answer which knob is used on which power and why.
Calculate total magnification by combining eyepiece × objective (e.g. ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective = 400×).
Decide whether a described circular feature is a cell or an air bubble and justify the answer.
activities.title: Check the procedure and the numeracy

feedback: If the learner draws the textbook cell rather than the view: record observation, not memory — include artefacts and folds as seen.
If the slide has bubbles or the image won't focus safely: revisit coverslip angle and the side-watching coarse-focus habit before retrying.
If an iodine stain is used and detail is lost in a dark wash: too much stain obscures structure — use a small amount, and if needed remake the mount.
If magnification is reported from one lens only: multiply eyepiece × objective.
activities.intendedInsight: Reliably obtaining and honestly recording a clear image of a well-made slide is the real target of the skill; fluency comes from doing it, not just describing it.
learnerActions: Prepare a real wet mount of a biological specimen (e.g. onion skin, using a drop of water or iodine stain as directed) and obtain a clear, bubble-free, correctly focused image.
Talk through each step while focusing, then increase magnification once the specimen is centred.
Make an accurate labelled line drawing with a scale, recording exactly what is seen.
State the total magnification used and, where sizes are given, work out magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
activities.title: Perform and record at the real bench
